title: Iran Says a Tiny Waterway Is as Powerful as an Atomic Bomb
summary: Did you know a skinny strip of water could be as powerful as a nuclear weapon? That's what some Iranian officials are saying about the Strait of Hormuz. This waterway is super important because about one-fifth of the world's oil passes through it every day. Recently, Iranian leaders have been talking a lot about how much control they have over this strait. One top adviser, Mohamad Mokhber, said it's "a capability on the level of an atomic bomb" because with one decision, Iran could affect the whole world's economy. Another official, Mohammad Reza Aref, said controlling the strait will help Iran fight back against U.S. sanctions, which are punishments that hurt its economy. This talk is happening while Iran and the U.S. are sending messages back and forth, trying to reach an agreement. The two countries have been in a tense standoff, and there have even been fights between Iranian and American ships near the strait. Iran's state TV compared the strait to a famous battle from early Islamic history, saying if Iran gives up control, it could lead to defeat. The new supreme leader, Mojtaba Khamenei, has also stressed keeping a grip on the waterway. But Iran also says it doesn't want to close the strait for no reason, because that would hurt Iran too. Still, the message is clear: Iran sees the Strait of Hormuz as a huge bargaining chip in its talks with the U.S.
why_it_matters: If the Strait of Hormuz ever became blocked, gasoline prices at your local pump could jump almost overnight, making it more expensive for your family to drive or for trucks to deliver food and toys.

keywords.explanation: A waterway is a narrow passage of water that ships use to travel, like a natural road on the sea.
The Strait of Hormuz is the skinny water passage between Iran and Oman that connects the Persian Gulf to the larger ocean.
Sanctions are penalties, often economic, that one country puts on another to force it to change its behavior.
A bargaining chip is something valuable you can offer or threaten to give up during a negotiation to get what you want.
A standoff is a situation where two sides cannot agree and neither wants to back down, creating a tense deadlock.
In Iran, the supreme leader is the highest political and religious authority, with more power than the president.

background_read: The Strait of Hormuz, located between Iran and Oman, is a narrow shipping route that carries about one-fifth of the world's oil every day.

Iran often points to this waterway as a powerful tool to pressure other countries, especially when facing U.S. sanctions—economic penalties meant to limit Iran's nuclear program and military activities.
The standoff with the U.S. goes back many years, and the strait has long been used as a bargaining chip in high-stakes negotiations.
Article_Structure: WHO: Iranian leaders such as adviser Mohamad Mokhber, First Vice President Mohammad Reza Aref, and the new supreme leader Mojtaba Khamenei.
WHAT: They are warning that Iran's control of the Strait of Hormuz is like having an atomic bomb and could be used as a bargaining chip against U.S. sanctions.
WHERE: The Strait of Hormuz, a narrow waterway in the Middle East between Iran and Oman.
WHY: Iran is trying to gain leverage in negotiations with the U.S. and to deter further economic pressure.

perspectives.description: Iranian leaders see the strait as a way to protect their country from outside pressure and to ensure their economy can survive sanctions.
Many countries say that turning a vital waterway into a weapon is dangerous and could trigger a military conflict that hurts everyone.
Energy experts point out that while Iran's threats are loud, actually blocking the strait would backfire by cutting off Iran's own oil exports and angering even its allies.
